title: Unusual spiral NGC 4921 in the Coma Galaxy Cluster
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 4921, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4921 · constellation Coma Berenices · about 250 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA and K. Cook (Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, USA)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: The spiral galaxy NGC 4921 sits in front of a rich backdrop of more distant galaxies in this very deep Hubble image. It belongs to the Coma Galaxy Cluster and lies about 250 million light-years away, in the constellation Coma Berenices.

A deep image is one that gathers light for a very long time, letting faint objects appear that a short exposure would miss. This one was assembled from a total of 80 separate pictures, taken through yellow and near-infrared filters and then combined.

The result shows two things at once. In the foreground is NGC 4921 itself, which astronomers describe as an unusual spiral. Behind it, across the rest of the frame, the long exposure picks up galaxies much farther away, each a system of stars in its own right, reduced by distance to small smudges and specks of light.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.20 x 3.27 arcminutes) and distance (250 million light years), the frame spans roughly 233,000 × 238,000 light-years. Its light set out about 250 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, built from yellow and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Combining 80 exposures reveals far fainter galaxies than any eye could detect, and part of the data is near-infrared light we cannot see.
